paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: The Black–Scholes model, also called Black–Scholes–Merton, is a mathematical model of a financial market that trades derivatives. It is named after the economists Fischer Black and Myron Scholes, and Merton, the first to write an academic paper about it, is sometimes credited too. At its heart is a partial differential equation, the Black–Scholes equation. From it comes the Black–Scholes formula, a theoretical price for options of the European style.

paragraphs.heading: Hedging the risk away
paragraphs.text: The main idea is hedging: buying and selling the underlying asset in a particular way so that risk is removed. For a European call or put, Black and Scholes showed one can hold the stock and sell the option short so that the combined position's value does not depend on the stock price. Rebalancing like this all the time is called continuously revised delta hedging. Because risk can be removed this way, the option has one unique price, given by the formula.

paragraphs.heading: The imagined market
paragraphs.text: The model assumes a market with at least one risky asset, usually a stock, and one riskless asset such as cash or a bond. The riskless asset earns a constant return, the risk-free interest rate. The stock price follows a geometric Brownian motion whose drift and volatility stay constant. There is no way to earn a riskless profit above the risk-free rate, anyone can borrow, lend, buy or sell any amount, even fractions, and no trade carries fees or costs.

paragraphs.heading: The one hidden number
paragraphs.text: Only one input to the formula cannot be read straight from the market: how volatile the underlying asset will be, on average, in the future. It can, though, be found from the prices of other options. Because an option is worth more when this volatility is higher, the formula can be run backwards to build a volatility surface. That surface is then used to calibrate other models.

paragraphs.heading: How it came about
paragraphs.text: Louis Bachelier's 1900 thesis was the earliest work to apply Brownian motion to pricing derivatives, though it had little impact for many years. In 1968 Black and Scholes showed that adjusting a portfolio over time removes the security's expected return, which gave birth to the risk-neutral argument. Merton was first to publish a paper widening the maths, and he coined the name Black–Scholes options pricing model. Merton and Scholes won the 1997 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences; Black had died in 1995 and could not receive it, but the Swedish Academy named him as a contributor.

paragraphs.heading: Its lasting impact
paragraphs.text: The formula set off a boom in options trading and gave the business mathematical legitimacy. Options traders still use the model widely, often with some adjustments. Its assumptions have since been loosened in many directions. Later versions allow for changing interest rates, transaction costs and taxes, and dividend payments.
